questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old male with a history of alcohol use presents with jaundice. His LFTs show: AST 320 U/L, ALT 140 U/L, ALP 180 U/L, GGT 520 U/L, bilirubin 5.4 mg/dL (direct 3.8 mg/dL). What is the AST:ALT ratio and what does it suggest?

options.C: Ratio = 1, suggesting non-alcoholic fatty liver disease

questions.explanation: An AST:ALT ratio >2 (here 320/140 = 2.28) is highly suggestive of alcoholic liver disease (ALD). This occurs because alcohol preferentially damages mitochondria (where AST is located) and depletes pyridoxal-5-phosphate (needed for ALT synthesis more than AST). Markedly elevated GGT is another hallmark of alcohol-related hepatic injury. In viral hepatitis, ALT typically exceeds AST (ratio <1) because hepatocyte cytoplasmic injury predominates. In ischemic hepatitis, both enzymes rise dramatically (>1000 U/L) with a ratio near 1.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old female presents with jaundice and confusion 7 days after an overdose of paracetamol (acetaminophen). She has no prior liver disease. PT is 38 seconds (INR 3.6), serum creatinine is 3.2 mg/dL, and bilirubin is 18 mg/dL. She is now encephalopathic (Grade III). Which criteria should be used to assess need for emergency liver transplantation?
questions.explanation: King's College Criteria (KCC) are used specifically for acute liver failure (ALF) to identify patients who require emergency liver transplantation. For paracetamol-induced ALF: pH <7.30 OR (INR >6.5 + creatinine >300 μmol/L + Grade III/IV encephalopathy — all three). This patient meets the triad (INR 3.6 approaches threshold, creatinine elevated, Grade III encephalopathy). MELD score is for chronic liver disease prioritization. Child-Pugh is for cirrhosis severity. N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol overdose if given within 8-10 hours.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old male with known alcoholic cirrhosis presents with confusion, asterixis (flapping tremor), and altered sleep-wake cycle. He recently started a high-protein diet and had a GI bleed last week. Serum ammonia is 142 μmol/L. EEG shows triphasic waves. What is the first-line treatment to reduce ammonia production in this patient?

options.B: Oral lactulose titrated to 2-3 soft stools per day

questions.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) results from accumulation of ammonia (produced by gut bacteria from protein/blood) bypassing the liver via portosystemic shunts. Precipitants here: GI bleed (protein load) and high dietary protein. First-line treatment is oral lactulose: it acidifies the colon (NH3 → NH4⁺, trapping ammonia), acts as a cathartic (reducing transit time), and alters gut flora. Target: 2-3 soft stools/day. Rifaximin is added for recurrent/refractory HE. Asterixis (negative myoclonus) and triphasic EEG waves are hallmarks of metabolic encephalopathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old male with liver cirrhosis and ascites presents with fever, abdominal pain, and worsening confusion. Diagnostic paracentesis shows: ascitic fluid PMN count 320 cells/mm³, ascitic fluid culture pending. Serum-Ascites Albumin Gradient (SAAG) is 1.3 g/dL. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Wait for culture results before starting antibiotics
options.B: Start empirical IV cefotaxime immediately + IV albumin infusion
options.C: Start oral ciprofloxacin and arrange outpatient follow-up
options.D: Perform therapeutic large-volume paracentesis and discharge

questions.explanation: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP) is diagnosed when ascitic PMN ≥250 cells/mm³ — treatment must NOT wait for culture results. Empirical IV cefotaxime (3rd generation cephalosporin) is first-line, covering enteric gram-negative organisms (E. coli, Klebsiella). IV albumin (1.5 g/kg on day 1, 1 g/kg on day 3) is mandatory as it prevents hepatorenal syndrome by expanding plasma volume and reducing bacterial translocation-induced inflammation. SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL confirms portal hypertension-related ascites. SBP carries ~30% in-hospital mortality; secondary prophylaxis with norfloxacin is given after recovery.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old male with decompensated cirrhosis is being evaluated for liver transplantation. His labs show: serum bilirubin 6.2 mg/dL, INR 2.4, serum creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, and serum sodium 128 mEq/L. The transplant team uses MELD-Na score for organ allocation. Which three parameters constitute the original MELD score formula?
questions.explanation: The MELD (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease) score uses: Bilirubin (hepatic excretory function), INR (hepatic synthetic function — coagulation factors), and Creatinine (renal function — hepatorenal syndrome marker). Formula: MELD = 3.78×ln[bilirubin] + 11.2×ln[INR] + 9.57×ln[creatinine] + 6.43. MELD-Na adds serum sodium (hyponatremia worsens prognosis). A MELD score >15 is the threshold where transplant benefit outweighs waiting list mortality. Child-Pugh uses albumin and PT instead of creatinine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 48-year-old male with a 20-year history of heavy alcohol use presents with acute jaundice, fever, tender hepatomegaly, and leukocytosis. Maddrey's discriminant function (MDF) is calculated as 58. Liver biopsy shows steatohepatitis with Mallory-Denk bodies, neutrophilic infiltrate, and pericellular fibrosis. What is the most appropriate pharmacological treatment?
questions.explanation: Severe Acute Alcoholic Hepatitis is defined by Maddrey's Discriminant Function (MDF) ≥32 (formula: 4.6 × [PT prolongation in seconds] + bilirubin in mg/dL). MDF ≥32 indicates high short-term mortality (>35% at 28 days without treatment). First-line treatment is oral prednisolone 40 mg/day for 28 days — it reduces hepatic inflammation and improves short-term survival. Response is assessed at day 7 using the Lille score. Pentoxifylline was previously used but large RCTs (STOPAH trial) showed no mortality benefit. Mallory-Denk bodies (cytokeratin aggregates) are characteristic of ALD.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 44-year-old obese male (BMI 34) with type 2 diabetes and hypertension is found to have elevated ALT (78 U/L) and hepatic steatosis on ultrasound during a routine health check. He drinks minimal alcohol (<10 g/day). Liver biopsy shows macrovesicular steatosis, lobular inflammation, hepatocyte ballooning, and perisinusoidal fibrosis (stage 2). What is the most effective intervention to reduce hepatic fibrosis progression in this patient?

options.C: Sustained weight loss of ≥7-10% body weight through diet and exercise

questions.explanation: This patient has NASH (Non-Alcoholic SteatoHepatitis) — the progressive form of NAFLD with inflammation, ballooning, and fibrosis. The only intervention proven to reduce hepatic fibrosis and achieve histological improvement in NASH is sustained weight loss of ≥7-10% of body weight. Lifestyle intervention (caloric restriction + 150-200 min/week exercise) remains the cornerstone of treatment. Vitamin E has modest benefit in non-diabetic NASH but not in diabetic patients. Metformin improves insulin resistance but does not reduce fibrosis. Ursodeoxycholic acid has shown no benefit in NASH trials.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old female presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting after a fatty meal. Serum amylase is 1,840 U/L and lipase is 2,200 U/L. CT scan shows peripancreatic fat stranding with no pancreatic necrosis. Revised Atlanta classification places her in the mild category. On day 3, she develops fever (38.8°C), rising WBC, and CT shows 40% pancreatic necrosis. Which scoring system best predicts severity and mortality in acute pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: The CT Severity Index (CTSI/Balthazar score) directly grades morphological severity on CT: it combines Balthazar grade (A-E based on peripancreatic inflammation) with degree of pancreatic necrosis (0%, <30%, 30-50%, >50%) to give a score of 0-10. CTSI >5 correlates with high morbidity and mortality. It is the best tool for assessing local complications (necrosis, abscess, pseudocyst). Ranson's criteria use clinical/lab parameters at admission and 48 hours. BISAP uses 5 bedside variables (BUN, impaired mental status, SIRS, age, pleural effusion) within 24 hours.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 17-year-old male presents with progressive jaundice, behavioral changes, and deteriorating academic performance. On slit-lamp examination, golden-brown rings are seen at the corneal periphery. Serum ceruloplasmin is 8 mg/dL (normal 20-40), 24-hour urine copper is 180 μg/day (normal <100), and liver biopsy shows elevated hepatic copper content (320 μg/g dry weight). His younger sister is asymptomatic. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of D-penicillamine in treating this condition?

options.A: Inhibits intestinal copper absorption by inducing metallothionein
options.B: Chelates copper forming a soluble complex excreted in urine
options.C: Directly inhibits ATP7B copper transporter dysfunction
options.D: Promotes biliary excretion of copper-albumin complexes

questions.explanation: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism (ATP7B gene mutation) causing toxic copper accumulation in liver, brain, and cornea. Kayser-Fleischer rings (corneal copper deposition) are pathognomonic. Biochemical triad: low ceruloplasmin, elevated 24-hr urine copper, elevated hepatic copper on biopsy. D-penicillamine is a copper chelating agent — it binds free copper to form a stable, soluble complex that is renally excreted, reducing tissue copper burden. Zinc acetate works differently — it induces intestinal metallothionein, blocking copper absorption. Used for presymptomatic/maintenance therapy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 62-year-old male with decompensated cirrhosis and tense ascites develops oliguria and rising creatinine (1.2 → 2.8 mg/dL over 48 hours) after a large-volume paracentesis without albumin replacement. Urine sodium is <10 mEq/L, urine microscopy is bland (no casts), and renal ultrasound is normal. There is no response to 48 hours of IV albumin (1 g/kg/day) challenge. Which vasoconstrictor agent is the first-line treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS) Type 1 (now AKI-HRS) is a functional renal failure in cirrhosis: rising creatinine, low urine sodium, bland urine microscopy, no response to volume challenge, normal renal imaging. Pathophysiology: severe splanchnic vasodilation → reduced effective arterial volume → compensatory renal vasoconstriction. First-line treatment: Terlipressin (V1 receptor agonist causing splanchnic vasoconstriction) + IV albumin (restores effective circulatory volume) — proven to reverse HRS in ~40-50% of patients. Terlipressin is superior to norepinephrine in non-ICU settings. Liver transplantation is the definitive cure. Dopamine has no proven benefit.
